Start here

Take the Titanic's bridge on the night of 14 April 1912. When the lookout rings three bells, the wheel and the telegraph are yours: turn her, slow her, or do neither. After the ice, run the clock faster under Time; its bar takes you back to any minute, to try another way.

The ice on a drawn night

The same berg, another watch

The 1912 orders as this model reconstructs them, on this berg: helm hard over away from the ice, reversed at the touch, engines stopped a minute later, with no engine order before the touch. The accounts of her engine orders differ, and Boxhall's "full speed astern" is not used. Only the moment of the order changes.

Order after the bellsWhat the ice does

Her handling is fitted to a consensus of the three sisters' trial record (Olympic, Titanic, Britannic). What the ice does to the plating is a model with fitted guesses: the plating's strength, the berg's mass, a bow that crushes at a force rising with the depth crushed. Read an outcome as an estimate. On its default the 1912 watch ends where she breaks, 2 h 36 min after the touch, as the model finds it (from the times witnesses gave, she broke between 2 h 35 min and just under 2 h 40 min after it, at about 2:15 to 2:19 am); carried on with no break to her foundering instead, a what-if the User Guide shows how to ask for, she founders 2 h 43 min after it.

Before the collision

Watertight doors

Murdoch closed the doors right after the collision. Open them and water spreads aft low in the ship instead of tipping the bow. The bridge's switch drops the doors at the tank top by electromagnets, so it needs current from the dynamos; a door falls shut in about 25 s. Without current, a float under each room's floor drops the doors into it when water comes in, and a lever at each door works by hand. A scenario's open doors are held open.

What depends on what

  • Coal
  • Fires
  • Steam
  • Engines
  • Turbine
  • Screws
  • Way
  • Steering
  • Dynamos
  • Doors
  • Pumps

Coal feeds the fires in six boiler rooms. Their steam drives the two reciprocating engines and the wing screws; the engines' exhaust drives the turbine and the centre screw, ahead only, with both engines above 40 rpm. The same steam works the steering engines that move the rudder, and the dynamos that light her and work the magnets that drop the watertight doors from the bridge. Water at a room's furnaces puts its fires out; water at an engine's crankshaft stops it; a screw or the rudder out of the water does nothing, and with no way on her the rudder has no water to work on. Without current a door's float still drops it when water reaches it. Her steam bilge pumps, 1,700 tons an hour in all, need steam and no current: on a watch the engineers put a room's own pumps on it when water comes in, and lead pumps from dry rooms to it through the bilge main half an hour later [bets on their practice]; a pump stops when the room it stands in floods. Against a big hole they buy minutes, not the ship.

Pumps

On a watch the pumps take your orders: a room's own pumps, every free pump that can reach it, or one pump, put on it; a pump or all of them taken off; or back to the engineers' rules. A pump on its own room works 5 minutes after the order, one led through the bilge main 30 minutes after it [bets, as the engineers' own: Wilding's "half an hour" to couple a pump to another room]. A room's suctions and the two mains limit what can be drawn from it; the peaks have no suction, and the holds' valves stood in the firemen's passage, lost once it floods (it was holed about 5 minutes after the collision in 1912). A pump stops when the room it stands in floods, and none works without steam. Each order goes in the watch's log, so "Replay my watch" gives it again, and the forecast runs the watch on with it.

Boiler rooms

RoomEnds litFiresCoal, t

An order to the stokehold: its stokers draw a room's fires in about twenty minutes [read]; the steam already raised carries the load a while longer. On a watch it goes in the log with the helm and telegraph orders.

Coal in her bunkers

Hours of coal with every boiler lit on the night at full firing; she burns less when she asks less of them. Applies on restart and to the next watch. With the bunkers empty a room's fires burn down in about fifteen minutes [bet].

What this is, and what it is not

Early access, a work in progress. This is a physics model of her sinking: the sea through her damage and over her bulkheads, her trim and list, her machinery and pumps, the encounter with the berg, and her fall to the bed, each computed step by step. The charts and tables below set the flooding against the 1912 record; her fall is set against the wreck as surveyed, where the page shows it. Where the record is silent the model makes a bet, and its code and notes name every bet.

It is not a record of the night. The people aboard are counted, not followed: no one's fate is shown. In the desktop app, if you switch on the crew's minds with your own key, their words are written by a language model, in character and from what had reached the bridge. They are not the men's words, and they are not the record. Her break is modelled as the moment her hull reaches its strength, where the model hands her to her fall, not as the tearing itself. Every time and figure on the page is the model's; this tab sets them against the record. The sources (the inquiries, her plans, the wreck surveys and the papers) are listed in the repository's SOURCES.md. Not affiliated with any other Titanic project.

How it works

The hull is a parametric fit to Harland & Wolff's hydrostatics (displacement, waterplane, KB, BM within about 1%), cut into 4,400 vertical columns. Every step integrates buoyancy and flood water over those columns at the ship's actual attitude. Sixteen compartments, split port and starboard and above and below E deck, exchange water through holes, doors and the open E deck using orifice and weir laws. Heave, pitch and roll are integrated as a damped rigid body. Its uncertain inputs (the opening's size, the flow laws, the pumps, the bunker and more) are calibrated by a history match against the 1912 record: of four thousand versions tried, thirty that pass the record's tests are kept, and one of them is the default. A count such as "k of 30" in this tab is over those thirty. They sample what the record does not rule out, and are not the whole of it. So the timeline table above is not a blind prediction: some of its rows helped fit the model, and the observation ledger in this tab says which.

What it leaves out, and where it misses

The tearing of her hull itself: the model finds the moment her bending and shear reach her strength and hands her to her fall there. From the times witnesses gave, she broke at about 2:15 to 2:19; some who watched saw her break, her second and third officers said she went down whole, and the wreck shows she broke. In the model she breaks flatter and farther forward than the wreck and the published analyses have her: at about 7 degrees of trim, where the analyses have 10 or more, and over boiler room 2, a few metres forward of boiler room 1, where she parted. Nothing is tuned to move it. Air trapped in her compartments while she floats: until her fall each space is open to the sea's pressure. The cause of her list to port late in the night, which Halpern's reconstruction from the witnesses puts at 10° to 15° (Rowe, the one witness with a figure, judged about 6° at 1:40): the model's own list is in the chart above. And her last minute on the 1912 damage card, which runs with no break: a roll onto her beam ends that no witness saw, a known fault of the model's end. Her superstructure's buoyancy is in: the decks above B deck float while dry and flood through their windows and stairways.

Sources: British Wreck Commissioner's report (compartment lengths, bulkhead decks); Halpern, A Matter of Stability and Trim and Lifeboats, Launch Times, List and Trim (2023); Wilding's evidence; Hackett & Bedford (RINA 1996).
